nameStory: The Tuberculated Crab Spider gets its name from the small bumps or 'tubercles' that dot its body like tiny hills on a landscape. The word tubercle comes from Latin meaning 'small swelling,' and these raised spots help distinguish it from its smoother crab spider cousins.
description: This small, angular spider is a master of disguise that hunts without building webs. Like other crab spiders, it can walk sideways and backwards with ease, holding its front legs wide like a crab's claws. The Tuberculated Crab Spider is typically brown or gray with a compact body that rarely exceeds 6mm in length. Its most distinctive feature is the bumpy texture created by small tubercles covering its body and legs.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, angular body with a distinctly bumpy texture from small raised tubercles that you can see with close inspection

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Variable brown to gray coloration with darker mottled patterns that help it blend with bark and plant debris

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small spider, typically 4-6mm in body length - about the size of a small peppercorn

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits motionless with front legs extended wide, waiting to ambush prey; moves in quick, jerky motions when disturbed

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web for catching prey - this is a sit-and-wait hunter that relies on camouflage and quick strikes

habitat: Found on tree bark, wooden fences, and plant stems where its bumpy texture and mottled coloration provide excellent camouflage. Prefers areas with rough surfaces that match its tuberculated appearance, from backyard gardens to woodland edges. Often spotted on oak, maple, and pine bark in both urban and rural settings throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hiding spots and begin hunting as temperatures warm. Look for them basking on sun-warmed bark surfaces.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible and actively hunting. Mating occurs during warm summer months.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, with females laying egg sacs before the first hard frosts arrive.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as eggs or young spiders in protected locations like bark crevices and leaf litter.

funFact: Despite being called a crab spider, the Tuberculated Crab Spider's bumpy skin texture actually makes it look more like a tiny piece of rough bark that sprouted legs - it's so well camouflaged that researchers sometimes locate them by gently brushing suspected bark surfaces and watching for movement!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small crab spiders, but the tubercles are the giveaway - run your finger gently over bark where you suspect one is hiding, and you'll feel the difference between a smooth spider and this bumpy species. Remember: 'Tuberculated equals textured.'
contextualKnowledge: This spider belongs to the genus Tmarus, sometimes called 'Octopus Spiders' because of their eight-legged sprawling hunting posture, though they're not related to octopi. The scientific name can be tricky - Tmarus is pronounced 'TEE-mar-us.'
compareHints: As the only Tmarus species commonly found in New England, compare it with other crab spiders in the Thomisidae family. Unlike the smooth Goldenrod Crab Spider or Whitebanded Crab Spider, the Tuberculated Crab Spider has its characteristic bumpy texture and prefers bark over flowers. Its angular, tubercled body immediately sets it apart from the rounded, smooth bodies of most other crab spiders.
